{{Short description|German chemist (born 1961)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=December 2021}}
'''Thomas Matthias Klapötke''' (born 24 February 1961) is a German [[inorganic chemist]] at [[LMU Munich]], studying explosives.

Klapötke was born in [[Göttingen]]; he grew up in Berlin and studied at [[Technische Universität Berlin]] (TU Berlin), completing his undergraduate degree in 1982, his [[PhD]] in 1986, and his [[habilitation]] in 1990. Klapötke worked as a lecturer at TU Berlin until 1995, when the [[University of Glasgow]] hired him for the [[William Ramsay|Ramsay]] professorship. Since 1997, Klapötke has worked at LMU Munich as a professor of Inorganic Chemistry.<ref name="CV">{{cite web|url=https://www.hedm.cup.uni-muenchen.de/personen/professors/klapoetke/index.html|last=Klapötke|first=Thomas&nbsp;M.|title=Prof. Dr. Thomas M. Klapötke|website=Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München}}</ref>

Klapötke's lab at LMU Munich is a group of about 30 employees, mainly studying explosives. Klapötke's goal is to generate "green" explosives, that either [[complete combustion|burn to completion]] or leave few toxic residues.<ref name="ZeitProfile" /><ref name="SDZProfile" /> [[Die Zeit]] called it "the only university laboratory in Germany investigating implements of war".<ref name="ZeitProfile">{{cite news|last=Albrecht|first=Harro|title=Mann mit Wumm|trans-title="The Man with Boom!"|work=[[Die Zeit]]|url=https://www.zeit.de/2008/18/P-Klapoetke|access-date=19 December 2021|language=de|quote=Thomas Klapötke leitet das einzige Hochschulchemielabor in Deutschland, das sich mit Wehrtechnik beschäftigt.}}</ref> For this reason, the [[Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution]] watches Klapötke's lab quite closely.<ref name="SDZProfile">{{cite news|author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.-->|title='Ich würde keiner Fliege etwas zuleide tun': Wehrtechnik an der LMU|language=de|trans-title="I wouldn't hurt a fly": Implements of war at LMU|date=7 September 2010|access-date=8 January 2022|work=[[Süddeutsche Zeitung]]|url=http://www.sueddeutsche.de/muenchen/wehrtechnik-an-der-lmu-die-gruene-bombe-des-professors-klapoetke-1.994523-2|quote=Nicht einmal Klapötkes Mitarbeiter kennen [die Formel].  Dabei werden alle überprüft. Vom Verfassungsschutz und von Klapötke selbst.}}</ref> Klapötke is funded both by the [[German federal government]] and the [[US military]]<ref name="SDZExpose">{{cite news|url=https://www.sueddeutsche.de/muenchen/geheimer-krieg-pentagon-sponsert-sprengstoffforschung-in-muenchen-1.1826790|access-date=8 January 2022|title=Pentagon sponsert Sprengstoffforschung in München: Geheimer Krieg|language=de|trans-title=The Pentagon Sponsors Explosives Research in Munich: Secret war|author=<!--Staff writer(s)/no by-line.-->|date=25 November 2013}}</ref> and has won a number of awards, including the 1986 [[Ernst Christian Friedrich Schering#Legacy|Schering Prize]].<ref name="CV" />  He is also one of the inventors of, and the namesake of the high-performing environmentally friendly high explosive [[TKX-50]], which has higher performances than conventional explosives like [[RDX]] and [[HMX]].
{{quote frame|But remember, N-amino [[azidotetrazole]] is the ''starting'' material for the work.  ...It's a base camp, familiar territory, merely a jumping-off point in the quest for still more energetic compounds. The most alarming of them has two carbons, ''fourteen'' nitrogens, and no hydrogens at all, a formula that even Klapötke himself, who clearly has refined sensibilities when it comes to hellishly unstable chemicals, calls ''exciting''.  ... [[1-Diazidocarbamoyl-5-azidotetrazole|The compound]] [link added] exploded in solution, it exploded on any attempts to touch or move the solid, and (most interestingly) it exploded ''when they were trying to get an infrared spectrum of it.''|[[Derek Lowe (chemist)|Derek Lowe]]|[https://www.science.org/content/blog-post/things-i-won-t-work-azidoazide-azides-more-or-less Things I Won't Work With: Azidoazide Azides, More Or Less]|9 January 2013}}
